doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: First paid gig at thirteen with high school players
summary: His first paid gig was a New Year's Eve at Wysocki's Restaurant with older high school musicians, whom he names.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: When you got out and started playing can you recall what kind of money you would have made?

My first gig, the first time I played for money I was 13 years old and we played at Wysocki’s Restaurant on New Year’s Eve in West Utica and it was a bunch of high school guys: Louie Angelini who I think is a professor of music at Utica College—
We didn’t call him Louie, we called him Gino. That’s ‘cause his parents called him Gino. He lived near me.

Played piano. Jimmy McIntyre, an alto saxophonist who I think ended up owning a music store somewhere near Richfield Springs or somewhere like that. Oh man — John Avolio, who I think became a music teacher and moved to Michigan, his father owned Avolio Electric near Proctor High School. The saxophonist was — gee I can’t remember his last name, good as I know him — he once came in the Five — he became a school teacher too and he became, well he came in the Five Spot once when I was working there, in 1959. He was surprised to see me, I was surprised to see him. I think he was teaching in Mount Vernon or somewhere in Westchester. They became music teachers. They were in high school and I was still in grade school, and they hired me to play this gig with them. Jimmy McGuire, that was the saxophonist’s name. Last I heard, quite a while ago, he owned a music store somewhere outside of Utica. But I guess by the time I was 16 I met Torrie and Ronnie Zito and I had started in high school taking auto mechanics, because one of my aunts said, “Well suppose you don’t make it in music, you’ve got to have something to fall back on.”
The old fall back on thing.
